standard.title: Communicating
standard.description: write and create texts to communicate findings and ideas for identified purposes and audiences, using scientific vocabulary and digital tools as appropriate
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can share questions, predictions, observations and ideas with others in simple forms (AC9S1I06, 1-2 band). They have not yet written or created texts that are explicitly structured for a purpose and audience, or used scientific vocabulary deliberately for communicative effect.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students write and create texts to communicate science findings and ideas for identified purposes and audiences, selecting appropriate text forms and scientific vocabulary, and using digital tools where appropriate.

nodes.label: Texts have purpose, audience and appropriate vocabulary
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a science text, its intended audience, and how purpose and audience influence the vocabulary and structure of the text.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify the purpose and audience of a given science text and explain at least one way the text is shaped by those factors.
nodes.typical_width: Students compare two texts communicating similar science content for different purposes or audiences (e.g. an informative report vs a persuasive poster) and identify structural and vocabulary differences.
wider: Examine how First Nations Australians share information about water sources or ecological knowledge using different forms — oral, visual, spatial — and discuss what each form communicates that others don't
Explore a range of text forms used in science communication (journal abstract, news article, infographic, documentary) and identify what purpose and audience each serves
Discuss how digital tools change what is possible in science communication — interactivity, multimedia, global reach
nodes.hinge_reason: Purpose-audience awareness is the prerequisite for deliberate text construction in Node 3. Students who have not internalised how purpose and audience shape vocabulary and structure default to a single writing style regardless of the task, making Node 3's selection-and-creation demand impossible to meet.

response_modes.reason: The purpose-audience-vocabulary relationship is non-obvious. Students default to a single writing style regardless of purpose or audience without scaffolding. Making the relationship explicit (who will read this → what do they need to understand → what vocabulary suits them → what structure helps them?) supports more deliberate text construction.

success_criteria: Identifies the purpose and audience of a given science text
Explains at least one way the text's vocabulary or structure is shaped by its purpose or audience

nodes.label: Using scientific vocabulary in writing
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use appropriate scientific vocabulary in their writing to communicate about science findings, selecting terms that are precise and appropriate for the purpose and audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Students use at least four science vocabulary terms accurately in a piece of written science communication.
nodes.typical_width: Students use scientific vocabulary purposefully — not just inserted, but used to communicate precise meaning that everyday words would not achieve — and explain the choice of at least one term.
wider: Produce an informative text using scientific vocabulary to explain the impact of introduced predators on food chains — applying U-strand vocabulary in an HE context
Construct a report using scientific vocabulary to explain which materials are best suited for particular products — connecting vocabulary from U04 to a written analytical task
Investigate how vocabulary use differs between a formal science report and a community-facing poster about the same topic — which terms stay, which are replaced, and why

response_modes.reason: Students tend to use scientific vocabulary as decoration rather than for precision — inserting terms without using them to carry meaning. Writing across multiple science contexts (food chains, water cycle, forces, materials) in different text forms helps students build a working sense of when scientific vocabulary adds precision and when simpler language suffices.

success_criteria: Uses at least four science vocabulary terms accurately and in context (not just listed)
At least one use of scientific vocabulary achieves precision that an everyday word could not

nodes.label: Selecting form and creating a text for purpose and audience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select an appropriate text form for a given science communication purpose and audience, and create a text in that form that communicates findings or ideas clearly.
nodes.minimum_width: Students create a text in a given form (informative text, poster, report, model) that communicates science findings for a specified purpose and audience.
nodes.typical_width: Students select and justify a text form for a given science communication purpose, create the text using appropriate vocabulary and structure, and evaluate whether the text achieves its purpose.
wider: Create a poster, song, slideshow or performance to encourage the school community to save water — choosing and justifying the form for the purpose and audience
Represent feeding relationships in multiple forms (written explanation, labelled diagram, physical model, oral presentation) and compare what each communicates most effectively
Use digital tools to create a multi-modal science text and discuss what the digital form allows that a written or drawn form cannot

response_modes.reason: Creating a science text for purpose and audience requires students to simultaneously apply vocabulary knowledge, form knowledge, purpose-audience reasoning, and their science content knowledge. All four dimensions must be coordinated in a single product. Students who have each element separately must now deploy them together — this is the integration challenge of the node.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The multi-form communication direction — representing the same findings in written, visual, and performance formats — offers genuine richness and connects to creative communication. The water conservation community text creates a genuine communicative purpose that gives students a real reason to think carefully about audience and form.
success_criteria: Creates a text in the specified or selected form that communicates the required science findings or ideas
Uses at least two science vocabulary terms accurately in the text
Text is structured appropriately for the identified purpose and audience
